applied.change: Fixed the convention rather than the two rows the reviewer named. schemas/skill.schema.json gains an optional `version_note` on a contract.standards row; tools/render_skill.py prints it as a footnote line under the Standards table so the Version column stays scannable; tools/validate_skills.py warns when `version` runs past 60 characters, naming version_note as the place the justification goes. The version value itself is never invented: each row keeps the version string a record already named, or reads 'unverified', and the entire original sentence moves verbatim into version_note, so no provenance is lost or reworded.

Swept every standards row in the repository over the 60-character threshold, not only xc-correlation and xc-idempotency-lease: 29 rows across 17 skills from waves 1 to 4b, including cap-telemetry, the donor the reviewer identified as the origin of the pattern. Short values are the token the record already names (`RFC 9457`, `RFC 8693`, `RFC 5545`, `revision 2026-07-28`, `draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07`, `1.11.0 (unverified)`, `Statement v1 (unverified)`, `v1.2 or later (unverified)`, `v1.1 or v1.0, unverified`, `pre-stable (unverified)`, `unversioned`) or plain `unverified` where the row's own note says no version is asserted. Every version_status stays `unverified`; nothing was fetched and no version was upgraded. The check was calibrated both ways: over cap-telemetry's pre-fix text it reports exactly its two rows at 211 and 224 characters, and over the fixed tree it is silent.

build-skill-authoring, which owns how a skill.json is written, now carries the convention as a proposed best practice: `version` holds the version string a record names or 'unverified', `version_note` holds which record named it, whether the specification was fetched and which skill owns the row, and the validator warns above 60 characters. The reviewer offered 'record the choice once so it stops looking like an oversight' as the alternative to fixing the rows; both were done, so the convention is stated where authors read it and enforced where they render.

lessons_for_next_section: A finding the reviewer calls a repo convention rather than a wave defect is the strongest kind: it means every skill that repeats it was written by an author who saw the pattern and copied it, so fixing only the two rows named would have taught the next author the wrong thing from fifteen other skills.

When a field is carrying two jobs -- a value and its justification -- split the field rather than shortening the prose. The schema change, the renderer footnote and the length warning together cost less than one more ceremony finding the same paragraph in a Version column.

Move the original text verbatim when you split a field. A short value plus the untouched sentence loses no provenance and invents no version; rewriting the justification while moving it is where a fetched-versus-search-only distinction quietly disappears.

Calibrate a new warning on the pre-fix text before trusting a clean run: the version check had to name cap-telemetry's two rows at 211 and 224 characters, and the empty-directory check had to name both directories, before either silence meant anything.

Dead scaffolding is a claim about content. An empty references/ tells a reader who opens it that the long material exists and they missed it; deleting the directory is the cheapest honest answer, and the check that finds it is three lines.
Two nits and no blocks is not a quiet ceremony. Both nits pointed at rules with no owner and no check; a section that produces only nits is where the discipline itself gets cheaper to strengthen.
